Problem 1: Predict a pump bearing failure within seven days so an engineer can schedule maintenance. Inputs are vibration, temperature and operating hours; the target is whether failure occurs within seven days. Historical sensor logs joined to dated maintenance records provide training data. Rare failures and missing maintenance labels limit reliability. ML is suitable if enough labelled failures exist; otherwise use manufacturer thresholds.
Problem 2: Predict tomorrow's electricity demand in kWh to plan a building's supply. Inputs are previous daily demand, occupancy, day of week and weather forecast; the target is next-day kWh. Smart-meter records and occupancy logs are plausible sources. Holiday changes and weather forecast errors may reduce accuracy. ML may capture changing demand patterns but must beat a simple previous-week baseline.
Problem 3: Calculate concrete volume from length, width and depth for a rectangular slab. Inputs are measured dimensions and the result is volume in cubic metres. Site measurements provide the data; measurement error is a limitation. ML is unnecessary because length times width times depth gives the required quantity directly.
Selected dataset: I choose building demand because meters provide repeated daily measurements with observable next-day targets. I would join daily occupancy and historical forecasts by date, check missing readings and units, and reserve the latest dates for evaluation. Actual future demand must never be an input. A small single-building sample may not represent other buildings, and occupancy must be aggregated to protect individuals.
